strengths: Well-motivated approach with compelling preliminary experiments (Figure 2) showing that DRL policies rank good actions highly even after distribution shift, effectively justifying the pruning-selection decomposition

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across discrete/continuous environments, ID/OOD test protocols, with proper ablation studies demonstrating both decomposition and MAML components contribute to performance
Addresses both generalization and adaptation together, a gap in prior work on online 3D-BPP
Consistent empirical improvements across multiple settings (1.3-1.8% OOD generalization, 0.9-2.2% OOD adaptation improvements)
Sound technical approach combining policy decomposition with MAML, with reasonable design choices (finetuning only selection policy during adaptation)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (MAML, policy decomposition, policy gradients); the contribution is mainly in application rather than algorithmic innovation
Modest empirical improvements especially for adaptation on ID datasets (0.2-0.9%), raising questions about practical significance and whether improvements exceed typical baseline variance

Circular dependency in pruning policy training (Eq. 2): using selection policy's actions to train the pruning policy lacks principled justification; why this objective is better than direct quality thresholds unexplained

Lack of theoretical justification: claims that pruning policy is 'domain-free' and selection is 'domain-specific' are only empirically observed; no formal analysis of why decomposition improves generalization

Incomplete draft with missing implementation details marked as 'details in ??' on pages 3-4; critical details missing including pruning threshold selection, specific MAML hyperparameters (α, β), and exact network architecture specs
Narrow scope limited to 3D bin packing with only item-size distribution shifts; generalization to other problems and shift types unclear; no computational cost analysis
Questionable motivation experiments (Figure 2b) assume known item distribution, which is unrealistic; adaptation experiments use only 1/300 of training data with limited analysis of sample efficiency

Marginal difference in ablations: ASAP w/o MAML sometimes achieves comparable or better adaptation than full ASAP (e.g., Table II OOD-Small: +2.1% vs +2.2%), suggesting MAML contribution may be overstated
No statistical significance testing or error bars provided; improvements of 0.3-0.9% on ID adaptation may not exceed baseline variance
Missing key analyses: no comparison with simpler baselines, no computational overhead evaluation, no sensitivity analysis for pruning ratio, no learning curves for adaptation efficiency

strengths: Well-motivated analysis of distribution shift problem: Figure 2 experiments clearly demonstrate that trained DRL policies rank good actions poorly under distribution shift, providing strong empirical motivation for the decomposition approach
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Testing on both discrete and continuous environments with both in-distribution and out-of-distribution datasets provides reasonable breadth
Clear problem formulation and distinction: The paper clearly separates generalization (w/o adaptation) from adaptation capability (w/ adaptation), making the contributions easier to interpret
Sensible use of ablation studies: ASAP w/o MAML and w/o Decouple variants help isolate component contributions
weaknesses: Incomplete submission with missing references: Multiple instances of '??' indicating unfilled citations on pages 2, 3, and 5 suggest the paper was submitted prematurely and unprepared for a major venue

Modest and statistically unvalidated improvements: Most generalization gains are 1-3% (often <1% on ID datasets) with no significance tests, confidence intervals, or error analysis. The practical significance of these improvements is unclear

Contradictory ablation results that undermine core claims: ASAP w/o MAML achieves better adaptation improvements than full ASAP on several datasets (e.g., OOD-Small discrete: +2.1% vs +1.5%), directly contradicting the motivation for MAML as a key contribution. The explanation of 'lower initial performance' is unsatisfying

Questionable technical design with circular dependencies: The pruning policy is trained on actions sampled by the selection policy (Eq. 2), not ground truth, creating a circular dependency. Claims that 'type I errors can be mitigated by the selection policy' are unsupported

MAML application lacks clarity and justification: Algorithm 1 treats distributions as tasks, but training uses only the Default distribution (Section V.A.c). Unclear how many distributions are sampled for meta-training or why this approach improves adaptation to different test distributions

Flawed adaptation evaluation setup: Using only 1/300 of training data is artificially limiting and not justified. This artificially biases comparisons toward ASAP (designed for quick adaptation) and may be insufficient for baselines without meta-learning to demonstrate adaptation capability

Missing critical technical details: Pruning threshold/ratio unspecified, no computational cost analysis for two-policy inference, network architecture underspecified (learning rates, sizes), hyperparameter sensitivity not explored

Limited novelty and narrow scope: Combines existing ideas (policy decomposition, MAML, finetuning) without fundamental innovation. Only evaluated on 3D bin packing with no comparison to domain randomization, data augmentation, or other meta-learning algorithms

Incomplete technical soundness: MCTS experiments only show 'slight performance drop' after pruning, which is weak evidence that pruned actions are 'inherently bad'. The claim that fixing the pruning policy generalizes better (Section IV.B) contradicts the core motivation about distribution shift

strengths: Well-motivated problem diagnosis: The preliminary experiments (Figure 2) effectively demonstrate that DRL solvers can identify bad actions but fail to rank good remaining actions after distribution shift, clearly justifying the proposed decomposition approach

Comprehensive and fair experimental evaluation: Thorough testing across discrete/continuous environments, in-distribution and out-of-distribution datasets, with proper ablation studies (w/o MAML, w/o Decouple) and meaningful baselines (PCT, AR2L, GOPT)

Addresses overlooked problem of rapid adaptation: Unlike prior work focused solely on generalization, this paper tackles the practical need for quick policy adaptation to new test distributions using only 1/300 of training data

Thoughtful technical design: Careful handling of Type I/II errors in pruning policy, principled two-phase training to avoid mutual interference, and consistent improvements across all experimental settings
Clear presentation and effective visualizations: Generally well-written with strong motivation figures; ablation studies clearly show the contribution of each component
weaknesses: Critical submission incompleteness: Multiple missing '??' placeholders undermine the paper, particularly the MCTS experiments that form the foundation of the pruning policy motivation (pages 2-3). These must be completed for the work to be reproducible and verifiable

Insufficient justification for keeping pruning policy fixed during adaptation: The claim that pruning policies learn 'more universal' top-K proposals lacks formal or empirical support. Why should a policy trained on Default distribution identify appropriate candidates for Small or Large distributions? This design choice needs stronger evidence

Incomplete online adaptation analysis: Algorithm 1 serves both initialization and adaptation despite different objectives. The advantage over simple finetuning of baseline methods with equivalent adaptation budget is never demonstrated. Comparison with standard SGD-based policy finetuning is missing

Modest and potentially insignificant improvements: Adaptation improvements range from +0.3% (Default) to +2.2% (OOD-Small), with no statistical significance testing (no error bars, confidence intervals, or hypothesis tests provided). Unclear if gains are meaningful or within noise

Limited theoretical justification: No formal analysis of why decomposition improves generalization. The intuition is reasonable but lacks rigor—no theoretical characterization of when this approach should succeed or fail

Narrow distribution shift evaluation: OOD datasets only vary item size ranges (e.g., [1,6] vs [6,11]). Real logistics scenarios may involve more dramatic shifts in aspect ratios, shape heterogeneity, or distribution characteristics—robustness to such shifts is untested

Missing technical details: How is pruning threshold k determined? What happens with empty/tiny pruned sets? Network architecture specifics, learning rates for different phases, and action sampling procedures during decoupled finetuning are not clearly described, hampering reproducibility

Incomplete MCTS validation: Paper claims 'only indicate slight performance drop' after pruning (page 3) but actual results are missing, making this critical validation inaccessible and reproducibility impossible

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clear identification and empirical demonstration of distribution shift issues in online 3D-BPP through MCTS experiments in Section 3.2
Intuitive and sound design: Policy decomposition into proposal and selection stages is well-justified and clearly presented with strong conceptual motivation

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Thorough experiments across discrete/continuous environments, multiple dataset variants (ID-Default, ID-Large/Medium/Small, OOD), proper baselines, and detailed ablation studies
Strong OOD generalization: Meaningful improvements on out-of-distribution datasets (1.3-2.2%) where baselines struggle, demonstrating practical value
Excellent reproducibility documentation: Detailed hyperparameters (Table 4), dataset generation procedures (Appendix A.4), experimental setup, and promise of code release
Solid experimental methodology: Proper comparison with relevant DRL baselines (PCT, AR2L, GOPT), includes timing analysis, and considers both generalization and adaptation capabilities
weaknesses: Lack of theoretical foundation: No theoretical analysis of why policy decomposition improves generalization or enables faster adaptation; claims about simplicity and generalizability lack formal justification
Modest improvement magnitudes: 2-4% improvements on in-distribution datasets and particularly small online adaptation gains (0.2-0.8% on ID, 0.9-2.2% on OOD) limit practical significance

Incomplete analysis of proposed mechanism: No investigation of what each policy learns, no visualization of which scenarios benefit from decomposition, and limited evidence that the proposal policy is truly domain-generalizable

Underexplored online adaptation design: Fixed proposal policy cannot adapt to new distributions; no analysis of failure modes, comparison with joint fine-tuning, or ablation isolating adaptation gains from baseline fine-tuning
Insufficient MAML justification: While MAML is used for pre-training initialization, limited analysis of why it helps beyond empirical results; no comparison with simpler initialization alternatives
Incremental novelty: Core contribution is architectural decomposition of existing DRL components; underlying techniques (GAT, policy gradients, MAML) are standard

Missing implementation details: Top-k selection procedure for proposals not detailed; exact selection policy architecture unspecified; number of random seeds for ASAP not reported; no error bars or confidence intervals
Limited scope: Restricted to online regular 3D-BPP with small containers (L=W=H=20); scalability to larger bins, irregular shapes, or other domains unexplored
Computational cost-benefit not well-articulated: Two-phase training adds 1 hour overhead, online adaptation adds 63 minutes; practical value of modest improvements against this cost unclear
Absent failure case analysis: No discussion of when approach fails or of fundamental mismatch between proposal and selection policies on challenging distributions

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (ID, OOD, discrete and continuous) with clear baselines and methodological setup
Well-motivated problem formulation addressing practical distribution shift in online 3D-BPP, with honest discussion of adaptation requirements
Clear presentation with effective use of figures to illustrate the core concepts and empirical findings
Consistent empirical improvements (1-4%) across most tested scenarios demonstrating robustness of the approach
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Policy decomposition into proposal and selection is intuitive but standard; the training procedure combines pre-training, meta-learning, and fine-tuning—all existing techniques with limited innovation

Weak theoretical justification: Paper shows DRL policies exhibit distribution mismatch but provides no principled analysis of why decomposition fundamentally addresses this. The connection between observation and proposed solution lacks rigor

Missing critical baseline comparison: Paper does not compare against simple fine-tuning of baseline methods (AR2L, GOPT). This is essential to determine if improvements come from decomposition or just from adaptation, fundamentally undermining the main claim

Modest empirical improvements without statistical significance testing: 1-4% gains across most cases, but with only ~64 test instances per subset and stochastic environments, statistical significance is never reported or verified

Misleading framing of contribution: Paper frames work as addressing 'generalization gap' but primarily demonstrates 'online adaptation'—a different problem where fine-tuning any method improves performance. The novelty claim is unclear

Proposal policy generalization not addressed: If proposal policy is fixed when facing very different distributions, it may generate poor candidates. Paper doesn't explore how far proposal policy generalizes or when both policies need updating

Limited insight into why decomposition works: Lacks analysis of what selection policy learns, how proposal policy performance varies across distributions, and when the approach fails (e.g., extreme distribution shifts)
Problem-specific contribution with unclear generalizability: Work is highly specialized to 3D-BPP with no demonstration of broader applicability to other combinatorial optimization or RL problems

Marginal contribution of proposed components: MAML appears to contribute minimally (Table 2 ablation shows only small differences), and the necessity of meta-learning given two-phase training is unclear
Incomplete ablation and analysis: Section 5.3 only compares ASAP variants; missing ablations on key design choices and no analysis of failure modes or domain-specific conditions affecting performance

strengths: Addresses a genuine and demonstrated problem: The paper provides convincing empirical evidence that DRL-based solvers suffer from distribution shift when encountering new item distributions, with clear evidence from the MCTS experiments in Section 3.2.

Principled technical approach: The decomposition into proposal and selection policies is well-motivated and theoretically justified. The observation that identifying promising actions is less distribution-dependent than selecting optimal actions provides solid theoretical grounding.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Evaluation across multiple datasets (ID/OOD, discrete/continuous), appropriate baselines (PCT, AR2L, GOPT), and rigorous ablations (Tables 1-2) demonstrate consistent improvements across diverse settings.
Well-designed two-phase training: Pre-training with meta-learning and post-training with coupled policies effectively avoids interference issues while promoting generalization and adaptation.

Practical and efficient: The approach only requires online fine-tuning of the selection policy, making it computationally feasible compared to full policy retraining. Time analysis shows acceptable overhead.

Strong generalization capability: Results show consistent performance improvements for both in-distribution and out-of-distribution scenarios, with particularly notable gains on challenging OOD datasets (1.3%-3.3% improvement range in Table 2).
Thorough reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters (Table 4), clear algorithms, promised code/data release, and comprehensive appendix support reproducibility.
Insightful ablation studies: Tables 1-2 clearly show that both policy decoupling and MAML pre-training are necessary for the method's success, with Tables 6-7 providing sensitivity analysis.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The method primarily combines existing components (Graph Attention Networks, policy gradient learning, MAML). The main contribution is architectural decomposition rather than novel algorithmic innovation.

Modest improvements in some cases: Gains range from 2-3% on certain in-distribution datasets (e.g., ID-Small in Table 1), raising questions about practical significance in some scenarios where baseline methods already perform well.

Narrow scope and limited generalization: Work is focused exclusively on 3D-BPP with cuboid items and standard constraints. Extension to other combinatorial optimization problems is mentioned but not demonstrated, limiting impact.

Increased inference time: The approach adds +40.4 minutes overhead on OOD-small dataset (Table 1), which could be prohibitive in time-critical applications. This practical limitation deserves more prominent discussion.

Proposal policy dependency: Success critically depends on MCTS generating sufficiently diverse promising actions. The paper lacks deep exploration of failure modes when the proposal policy struggles or analysis of proposal policy generalization properties.

Incomplete analysis of decomposition benefits: While the paper shows the decomposition works, deeper investigation into why identifying promising actions is more generalizable than selecting optimal actions would strengthen the contribution.

Some experimental design choices lack justification: The selection of specific k values (3, 5, 8, 10) for sensitivity analysis in Tables 6-7 and the rationale for certain MCTS parameters could be better explained.
